vignette:
Layla is a 38-year-old school principal, a divorced mother of two, who served a tour in a combat zone a decade ago. The event that fractured her sense of safety occurred during a routine convoy: an improvised explosive device detonated beside her vehicle, followed by small-arms fire. In the chaos, she remembers the deafening blast, the screams of her comrades, and the sickening realization that the soldier next to her had been hit. She cannot piece the sequence together in her mind-the memories jump from the flash of light to the sight of blood to the sound of her own shouting, without any clear order. What returns most vividly, and most often, is the auditory recall: the crack of gunfire and the metallic ring of the explosion replay in her head, sometimes triggered by a car backfiring or a door slamming.

Since the event, Layla has come to believe that people cannot be trusted. She saw fellow soldiers turn on each other under pressure, and she now applies that lesson to everyone around her. At school, she keeps her office door locked and scrutinizes the motives of her staff, certain that they are hiding something. This pervasive mistrust has hollowed out her life; nothing feels meaningful anymore. She describes her work as a series of mechanical tasks, devoid of the passion she once had. Her reactions since the trauma-the hypervigilance, the rage that surges when she recalls the event-have convinced her that she is a lousy coper, that she should have been able to move on by now.

This belief in her own inadequacy directly fuels her sense of threat. Because she sees herself as weak, she constantly scans for danger, believing she cannot handle what might come. At home, she is always on guard, even inside her own four walls. She cannot sit with her back to a door; before she feels comfortable anywhere, she identifies every escape route. The school hallways, once familiar, now feel like a trap. She walks with her keys between her fingers, her eyes darting to exits. The memories themselves intensify this state: when the auditory recall hits-hearing the explosion again-the rage that follows is so consuming that she feels she could lash out, and that loss of control terrifies her, making her even more vigilant.

The reciprocal cycle is tight: her heightened threat monitoring primes her to notice any sound that resembles the trauma, which drags her back into the memory. Each time she hears a sudden loud noise, the confusion and rage return, and she mentally replays the event. This, in turn, reinforces her negative appraisals. She tells herself, "I can't even be in my own house without panicking-I really am a bad coper." That self-judgment then justifies more scanning, more escape planning, and more isolation. Her divorce, which occurred two years after her deployment, she now interprets as further proof that she cannot be trusted with relationships, that she is fundamentally broken.

Over the months, her avoidance has become a way of life. She has stopped going to the grocery store, relying on delivery instead, because the crowds feel too unpredictable. She no longer accepts invitations to social gatherings with other school administrators, fearing someone will ask about her past. The consequences have been concrete: her performance reviews at work have slipped, and the school board has noted her reluctance to attend public events. Her children have begun to ask why she never takes them to the park anymore. She told her therapist in the first session that she is exhausted, that she is tired of looking over her shoulder, and that she came because she is afraid her anger will one day erupt at the wrong person-a child, a teacher, a stranger. What she hopes for, she said quietly, is to feel like she belongs in her own life again.
